history: Vulpecula, the Little Fox, has no ancient myth. It was invented by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius of Danzig (Gdansk), who introduced it in his star catalogue of 1687 to fill a gap of faint, unclaimed stars between the Swan and the Eagle. His star atlas, published in 1690 after his death, shows a fox running with a goose clamped in its jaws.

Hevelius explained his choice. He put the fox beside two other hunting creatures of the sky, the Eagle (Aquila) and the Vulture (an old alternative picture for Lyra), and he said the fox was carrying the goose to Cerberus, the three-headed dog he had drawn nearby in the hand of Hercules. Cerberus has since been dropped from the sky, so that part of the scene is lost.

The name took a while to settle. Hevelius called the pair 'Vulpecula cum Ansere', the little fox with the goose, in his catalogue, but labeled them separately as Anser and Vulpecula on his atlas; other astronomers wrote 'the Fox and Goose'. In 1845 the English astronomer Francis Baily shortened it to Vulpecula alone. The goose has not quite vanished: in 2017 the constellation's brightest star, [[star:α Vul|Alpha Vulpeculae]], was officially named Anser.

overview: Vulpecula is a small fox drawn by a 17th-century astronomer from a scattering of faint stars in the middle of the Summer Triangle. It has no recognizable shape and no bright stars, but it holds two favorite targets for beginners: the Coathanger and the Dumbbell Nebula.
howToFind: Do not look for a fox; look for a place. Vulpecula is the strip of sky inside the [[asterism:summer-triangle|Summer Triangle]] that lies just south of [[star:Albireo|Albireo]], the star at the foot of the Northern Cross, and just north of the little arrow of [[con:Sge|Sagitta]]. Its brightest star, [[star:α Vul|Anser]], is three degrees (two finger-widths) south of Albireo. It is in the evening sky from June into November.

The two showpieces are easier to find from Sagitta. For the Coathanger, [[dso:Cr399|Brocchi's Cluster]], sweep binoculars about four degrees northwest of the arrow's feathers ([[star:α Sge|Alpha Sagittae]]); it is also one third of the way from [[star:Altair|Altair]] to [[star:Vega|Vega]]. For the Dumbbell Nebula, [[dso:M27|M27]], go three degrees due north from the arrow's tip, [[star:γ Sge|Gamma Sagittae]].
shape: There is no pattern to see: just a zigzag of fourth- and fifth-magnitude stars about two fists long (magnitude is the brightness scale, where smaller numbers are brighter). From a city none of them is visible to the naked eye, and even in the country the constellation is known for what it contains rather than how it looks.

mainStars.note: Anser, 'the goose', a red giant of magnitude 4.4 about 290 light-years away, and the only star in the constellation with a Greek letter. Binoculars show it as a wide pair with a fainter, unrelated star.

notableObjects.note: The Coathanger, or Brocchi's Cluster: ten stars that form a perfect upside-down coat hanger, a straight bar of six with a hook of four. It is a chance alignment rather than a true cluster, and one of the most delightful binocular sights in the sky, even from a city.

The Dumbbell Nebula, the glowing shell of gas thrown off by a dying star, and the first object of its kind ever found (by Charles Messier in 1764). Binoculars under a dark sky show a small dim patch; a small telescope shows its two-lobed shape, like an apple core or an hourglass.

A rich open cluster in the eastern part of the constellation, toward the wing of Cygnus. From a dark site binoculars show a faint elongated haze that a small telescope resolves into dozens of dim stars.

facts: The first pulsar, a spinning collapsed star that sends out a radio pulse every 1.3 seconds, was discovered in Vulpecula in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell at Cambridge.
The Coathanger was first recorded by the astronomer al-Sufi in 964 CE, long before the constellation around it existed.
'The Fox and Goose', one of the constellation's old names, is also a traditional name for pubs in Britain.
